quote: are by inducing inflammation, inducing antiviral defense, and stimulating adaptive immunity

quote: gain-of-function mutations of NOD2 that cause increased NOD signaling and NF-κB activation lead to a systemic inflammatory disease called Blau syndrome

fact: Blau syndrome causes spontaneous inflammation in the joints, eyes and skin.
quote: Blau syndrome, which is characterized by spontaneous inflammation in the joints, eyes, and skin.

fact: Inflammasomes are cytosolic multiprotein complexes that form in response to infection or cell injury and generate active caspase-1.
quote: Inflammasomes are multiprotein enzymatic complexes that form in the cytosol in response to infections or cell injury

fact: Oligomerized NLRP3 binds the adaptor ASC; ASC filaments recruit procaspase-1, which clusters and becomes active caspase-1.

quote: the main function of caspase-1 is to cleave the inactive cytoplasmic precursor forms of IL-1β and IL-18.

fact: IL-1β lacks a signal peptide; caspase-1 cleaves gasdermin D, and the N-terminal fragment forms plasma membrane pores through which IL-1β leaves the cell.

fact: NLRP3 senses uric acid crystals, alum, cholesterol crystals, extracellular ATP, silica, streptococcal and staphylococcal toxins, and influenza virus.
quote: uric acid crystals, aluminum hydroxide crystals used in vaccine adjuvants, cholesterol crystals, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) released from mitochondria, silica

fact: Common upstream triggers of NLRP3 are reduced cytosolic K+ (K+ efflux) and reactive oxygen species; crystals may act by damaging lysosomal membranes.

fact: The adjuvant effect of aluminium hydroxide (alum) depends on NLRP3 and the inflammasome pathway.
quote: aluminum hydroxide (alum) rely on NALP3 and the inflammasome pathway

fact: Pyroptosis is an inflammatory programmed cell death of macrophages and dendritic cells, but not neutrophils, caused by gasdermin D pores; fluid enters, the cell swells and the plasma membrane fails.
quote: an inflammatory form of programmed cell death of macrophages and DCs (but not of neutrophils and most other cell types) called pyroptosis

fact: In the noncanonical pathway, cytosolic LPS activates caspase-4 or caspase-5 in humans (caspase-11 in rodents), which cleaves gasdermin D and causes pyroptosis.
quote: uses a different caspase (caspase-11 in rodents; caspase-4 or caspase-5 in humans)

fact: Other inflammasome sensors are NLRC4 (cytosolic flagellin, type III secretion system), NLRP1 (anthrax lethal toxin), AIM2 (dsDNA) and pyrin (toxins that modify Rho GTPases).
quote: NLRC4 recognizes cytosolic flagellin and components of the type III secretion system of bacteria. NLRP1 recognizes the anthrax lethal toxin.

fact: Phagocytosed monosodium urate crystals damage lysosomes and activate inflammasomes; IL-1 antagonists are used for severe gout resistant to conventional drugs.
quote: IL-1 antagonists have been used to effectively treat cases of severe gout that are resistant to conventional anti-inflammatory drugs.

fact: Gain-of-function mutations in inflammasome components, or loss-of-function mutations in their regulators, cause excess IL-1 with recurrent fever and inflammation of skin, joints and abdomen (inflammasomopathies, a subgroup of autoinflammatory syndromes).
quote: due to autosomal gain-of-function mutations in one or another of their component proteins or loss-of-function mutations in their regulators

fact: Autoinflammatory diseases differ from autoimmune diseases, which are caused by self-reactive antibodies and/or T cells.
quote: Autoinflammatory diseases are distinct from autoimmune diseases, which are disorders of adaptive immunity caused by antibodies and/or T cells reactive with self antigens.

fact: Mutations in NLRP3 (cryopyrin) cause cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS).
quote: Autoinflammatory diseases caused by mutations in NLRP3 (also known as cryopyrin) are called cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS).

fact: Patients with CAPS can be treated successfully with IL-1 antagonists.
quote: Patients with CAPS can be successfully treated with IL-1 antagonists

fact: CAPS is caused by gain-of-function NLRP3 mutations and presents with fever, neutrophilic rash, bony lesions and central nervous system inflammation.
quote: Fever, neutrophilic rash, bony lesions, central nervous system inflammation

fact: Muckle-Wells syndrome and familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (FCAS) are dominantly inherited NLRP3 disorders with fever (cold-induced in FCAS), urticarial rash, joint pain and conjunctivitis.
quote: episodes of fever—which is induced by exposure to cold in the case of FCAS—as well as urticarial rash, joint pains, and conjunctivitis

fact: Muckle-Wells syndrome also causes progressive deafness.
quote: Periodic fever, urticarial rash, joint pains, conjunctivitis, progressive deafness

fact: NLRP3 mutations also cause chronic infantile neurologic cutaneous and articular syndrome (CINCA), with neonatal-onset fever, urticarial rash, arthropathy and neurological disease.
quote: Mutations in NLRP3 are also associated with the autoinflammatory disorder chronic infantile neurologic cutaneous and articular syndrome (CINCA)

fact: Muckle-Wells syndrome responds dramatically to anakinra, an IL-1 receptor antagonist.
quote: Muckle–Wells syndrome responds dramatically to the drug anakinra, an antagonist of the receptor for IL-1.

fact: Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is caused by mutations in MEFV, which encodes pyrin; it presents with fever, serositis and arthritis.
quote: familial Mediterranean fever, caused by mutation of the MEFV gene, which encodes pyrin.

fact: TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS) is caused by mutations in the gene for TNF receptor I, gives periodic fever, myalgia and rash, and responds to TNF blockade.
quote: (TRAPS) is caused by mutations in quite a different gene, that encoding the TNF-a receptor TNFR-I.

fact: Hyper-IgD syndrome (HIDS) is caused by partial mevalonate kinase deficiency and gives fever from infancy, high serum IgD and lymphadenopathy.
quote: is caused by mutations that result in a partial deficiency of mevalonate kinase

fact: RIG-like receptors (RLRs) are cytosolic sensors of viral RNA that induce type I IFNs; the best known are RIG-I and MDA5.
quote: RIG-like receptors (RLRs) are cytosolic sensors of viral RNA that respond by inducing the production of the antiviral type I IFNs

fact: MDA5 recognizes long dsRNA (1-6 kb).
quote: MDA5 recognizes long dsRNA (1–6 kb)

fact: RIG-I recognizes RNA with a 5′-triphosphate, which host cytosolic mRNA does not have because of its 7-methylguanosine cap.
quote: RIG-I will only recognize RNA with a 5′ triphosphate moiety

fact: SARS-CoV-2 RNA vaccines use pseudouridine instead of uridine to reduce detection by innate RNA sensors.
quote: changing uridines to derivatives called pseudouridines, which reduced detection by innate RNA sensors

fact: Activated RLRs bind MAVS on the outer mitochondrial membrane; MAVS polymerizes and recruits TRAF proteins that activate TBK1 and IKK.
quote: the RLRs are recruited to the outer mitochondrial membrane by the MAVS (mitochondrial antiviral-signaling) protein

fact: TBK1 phosphorylates IRF3 and IRF7, and IKK activates NF-κB; these transcription factors induce type I IFNs.
quote: TBK1 phosphorylates and activates IRF3 and IRF7 and IKK activates NF-κB; these transcription factors induce production of type I IFNs.

fact: RIG-I-deficient mice are susceptible to several ssRNA viruses but not picornaviruses; MDA5-deficient mice are susceptible to picornaviruses.
quote: mice deficient in MDA-5 are susceptible to picornaviruses, indicating that these two sensors of viral RNAs have crucial but distinct roles

fact: Cytosolic DNA sensors detect dsDNA from microbes or damaged host cells (micronuclei, mitochondria) and induce type I IFN and autophagy.
quote: Cytosolic DNA sensors (CDSs) are molecules that detect double-stranded (ds) DNA in the cytosol

fact: Cytosolic dsDNA activates the enzyme cGAS, which makes the second messenger cyclic GMP-AMP (cGAMP).
quote: cytosolic dsDNA activates the enzyme cGAS (cyclic guanosine monophosphate–adenosine monophosphate [GMP-AMP] synthase), which generates a signaling molecule called cGAMP

fact: STING is an endoplasmic reticulum adaptor that binds cGAMP, moves to the Golgi and activates TBK1, which activates IRF3/IRF7 and NF-κB to induce type I IFN.
quote: STING is an endoplasmic reticulum–localized transmembrane adaptor protein whose cytosolic tail binds to cGAMP with high affinity

fact: Gain-of-function STING mutations cause a type I IFN-driven systemic inflammatory disease of skin and lung (an interferonopathy).
quote: Gain-of-function mutations in the gene that encodes STING result in systemic inflammatory disease with manifestations in skin and lung

fact: STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy (SAVI) presents with cutaneous vasculopathy, fever and interstitial lung disease.
quote: Cutaneous vasculopathy, fever, and interstitial lung disease

fact: Aicardi-Goutières syndrome is an interferonopathy caused by loss-of-function mutations in nucleases (e.g., TREX1, SAMHD1), so excess nucleic acid reaches the sensors.
quote: Loss of function mutations in genes encoding DNAases and RNAases, excessive DNA and RNA available to nucleic acid sensors

fact: AIM2 binds cytosolic dsDNA and forms an inflammasome that generates active IL-1β.
quote: AIM2 (absent in melanoma-2) is another cytosolic sensor that binds cytosolic dsDNA and forms an inflammasome

fact: The mannose receptor (CD206) on macrophages mediates phagocytosis of microbes with terminal mannose, fucose or N-acetylglucosamine; host glycans usually end in galactose and sialic acid.
quote: eukaryotic cell surface carbohydrates are most often terminated by galactose and sialic acid

fact: Dectin-1 (CD369) binds fungal β-glucan and is required for immunity to Candida, Aspergillus and Pneumocystis.
quote: Dectin-1 (CD369) binds β-glucan, which is a major cell wall component of many fungal species

fact: Dectin-1 and Dectin-2 signal through an ITAM/SYK/CARD9 pathway to NF-κB and promote Th17 differentiation and antifungal immunity.
quote: ITAM/SYK/CARD9 pathway of NF-κB activation

fact: Scavenger receptors such as SR-A and CD36 on macrophages mediate phagocytosis; CD36 is a co-receptor for TLR2/6.
quote: CD36 functions as a coreceptor in TLR2/6 recognition and response to bacterially derived lipoteichoic acid and diacylated lipopeptides

fact: Formyl peptide receptor 1 (FPR1) on leukocytes recognizes N-formylmethionyl peptides, which bacteria and mitochondria make, and directs cell movement.
quote: synthesis of all bacterial proteins and few mammalian proteins (only those synthesized within mitochondria) is initiated by N-formylmethionine

fact: Pentraxins are the short pentraxins CRP and serum amyloid P (SAP) and the long pentraxin PTX3.
quote: the short pentraxins, C-reactive protein (CRP) and serum amyloid P (SAP), and the long pentraxin PTX3

fact: CRP binds phosphorylcholine and SAP binds phosphatidylethanolamine on bacteria and apoptotic cells.
quote: The ligands recognized by CRP and SAP include phosphorylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, respectively

fact: CRP, SAP and PTX3 all activate the classical complement pathway by binding C1q.
quote: CRP, SAP, and PTX3 all activate the classical pathway of complement by binding C1q.

fact: Plasma CRP can rise up to 1000-fold in infection because IL-6, IL-1 and TNF increase its synthesis in the liver.
quote: Plasma concentrations of CRP are very low in healthy individuals but can increase up to 1000-fold during infections

fact: PTX3 is made by dendritic cells, macrophages and endothelial cells, is stored in neutrophil granules and protects mice against Aspergillus fumigatus and influenza.
quote: PTX3 is also stored in neutrophil granules and released as neutrophils die.

fact: Mannose-binding lectin (MBL) is a collectin that binds terminal mannose and fucose and acts as an opsonin; low MBL levels increase infection risk, mainly with other immune defects.
quote: Low MBL levels result in increased susceptibility to a variety of infections, especially in individuals who have other immune defects.

fact: MBL triggers the lectin pathway of complement through MASP1 and MASP2.
quote: The lectin pathway is triggered by a plasma protein called mannose-binding lectin (MBL)

fact: The collectins SP-A and SP-D in lung alveoli bind microbes and act as opsonins for alveolar macrophages.
quote: They bind to various microorganisms and act as opsonins, facilitating ingestion of the microbes by alveolar macrophages.

fact: Ficolins have a fibrinogen-type (not C-type lectin) recognition domain, bind N-acetylglucosamine and lipoteichoic acid, opsonize bacteria and activate complement like MBL.
quote: instead of a C-type lectin domain, they have a fibrinogen-type carbohydrate recognition domain

fact: TNF, mainly from macrophages, activates endothelium and neutrophils, induces acute-phase proteins and fever, and causes cachexia and apoptosis.
quote: Muscle, fat: catabolism (cachexia)

fact: IL-1 activates endothelium, causes fever, induces acute-phase proteins and promotes Th17 differentiation.
quote: Endothelial cells: activation (inflammation, coagulation) Hypothalamus: fever Liver: synthesis of acute-phase proteins T cells: Th17 differentiation

fact: IL-6 induces acute-phase reactants in the liver and promotes differentiation of IL-17-producing helper T cells.
quote: It induces the synthesis of acute-phase reactants by the liver and promotes the differentiation of IL-17–producing helper T cells.

fact: IL-12 from dendritic cells and macrophages stimulates IFN-γ production by ILC1s, NK cells and T cells and promotes Th1 differentiation.
quote: it stimulates IFN-γ production by ILC1s, NK cells, and T cells; enhances NK cell–and CTL-mediated cytotoxicity; and promotes differentiation of Th1 cells

fact: Patients with IL-12 receptor β1 mutations are highly susceptible to Salmonella and mycobacteria.
quote: patients with mutations in the IL-12 receptor β1 subunit are highly susceptible to infections with intracellular bacteria, notably Salmonella and mycobacteria

fact: IL-18, like IL-1, needs the inflammasome for activation; it enhances NK cell functions.
quote: IL-18 enhances the functions of NK cells, similar to IL-12.

fact: Type I IFNs induce an antiviral state and increase MHC class I expression in all cells, and activate NK cells.
quote: All cells: antiviral state, increased MHC-I expression

fact: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are the major source of IFN-α; many cell types make IFN-β.
quote: Plasmacytoid DCs are the major sources of IFN-α

fact: TNF and IL-1 stimulate secretion of the chemokines CXCL8 and CCL2, which attract neutrophils and monocytes respectively.
quote: TNF and IL-1 also stimulate various cells to secrete chemokines, such as CXCL8 and CCL2, which bind to receptors on neutrophils and monocytes, respectively.

fact: TNF, IL-1 and IL-6 induce hepatocytes to produce acute-phase proteins, including CRP, SAP and fibrinogen.
quote: TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 induce hepatocytes to produce acute-phase proteins, including CRP, SAP, and fibrinogen

fact: Septic shock is mediated in large part by TNF.
quote: Septic shock, a life-threatening condition resulting from severe infections, is mediated in large part by TNF.

fact: IL-33 is stored in the nuclei of barrier epithelial cells and acts as an alarmin when damaged cells release it.
quote: It is often called an alarmin because it is rapidly released from damaged epithelial cells

fact: Mast cells express TLRs, and TLR ligands can induce mast cell degranulation.
quote: Mast cells express TLRs and TLR ligands can induce mast cell degranulation.

fact: In the allergy chapter, TLR ligands are listed among stimuli that make mast cells produce lipid mediators, cytokines and chemokines without degranulation.
quote: These stimuli include Toll-like receptor (TLR) ligands; substances released from injured cells, including ATP; fungal glucans

fact: Some DAMPs act through TLRs: heat shock proteins bind TLR4 and HMGB1 binds TLR2.
quote: heat shock proteins (HSPs), which are chaperones induced in response to various cell stresses and bind to TLR4

fact: Type I IFNs from virus-exposed cells act mainly on uninfected neighbouring cells to prevent spread of the virus.
quote: act mainly on other uninfected cells to prevent the spread of viral infection

fact: The MyD88–IRAK4–IRAK1 pathway lies downstream of most TLRs and of the IL-1 receptor and induces proinflammatory cytokines through NF-κB.
quote: The major signaling pathway downstream of most TLRs and of the IL-1 receptor (IL-1R) includes the MyD88 adaptor and the IRAK-4 and IRAK-1 kinases

fact: Janeway describes FMF as autosomal recessive and proposes that absence of functional pyrin leads to unregulated cytokine activity.
quote: It is proposed that an absence of functional pyrin leads to unregulated cytokine activity and defective apoptosis

fact: STING directly senses the bacterial second messengers cyclic di-GMP and cyclic di-AMP.
quote: The bacterial second messenger molecules cyclic di-GMP (c-di-GMP) and cyclic di-AMP (c-di-AMP) are directly sensed by STING.

fact: Selectins mediate the first, low-affinity adhesion of circulating leukocytes to endothelial cells of postcapillary venules.
quote: Selectins are plasma membrane carbohydrate-binding adhesion molecules that mediate an initial step of low-affinity adhesion of circulating leukocytes

fact: Endothelial cells express P-selectin (CD62P) and E-selectin (CD62E).
quote: Endothelial cells express two types of selectins, called P-selectin (CD62P) and E-selectin (CD62E).

fact: Leukocytes, not endothelial cells, express L-selectin (CD62L).
quote: A third selectin, called L-selectin (CD62L), is expressed on leukocytes and not on endothelial cells.

fact: P-selectin is stored in endothelial granules and moves rapidly to the luminal surface in response to histamine and thrombin.
quote: is stored in cytoplasmic granules of endothelial cells and is rapidly redistributed to the luminal surface in response to histamine from mast cells

fact: IL-1 and TNF induce E-selectin expression on endothelial cells within 1 to 2 hours.
quote: E-selectin is synthesized and expressed on the endothelial cell surface within 1 to 2 hours in response to the cytokines interleukin-1 (IL-1)

fact: The best-defined leukocyte ligand for E-selectin and P-selectin is the tetrasaccharide sialyl Lewis X.
quote: The best defined of these is the tetrasaccharide sialyl Lewis X

fact: PSGL-1 on leukocytes displays sialyl Lewis X, the major carbohydrate ligand for P-selectin.
quote: P-selectin glycoprotein ligand 1 (PSGL-1) is posttranslationally modified to display sialyl Lewis X, which serves as the major carbohydrate ligand for P-selectin

fact: Endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies contain preformed P-selectin.
quote: induce the rapid externalization of granules called Weibel-Palade bodies in the endothelial cells. These granules contain preformed P-selectin

fact: Selectin-ligand bonds have low affinity and a fast off-rate, so they form and break repeatedly and the leukocyte rolls.
quote: the interactions of selectins with their ligands are of low affinity (Kd ~100 μm) with a fast off-rate

fact: Integrins are heterodimers of one alpha chain and one beta chain.
quote: all of which are heterodimers containing 1 of 18 types of α chains and 1 of 8 types of β chains

fact: LFA-1 (CD11aCD18) binds ICAM-1 (CD54) on cytokine-activated endothelium.
quote: One important ligand for LFA-1 is intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1, CD54), a membrane glycoprotein expressed on cytokine-activated endothelial cells

fact: MAC-1 (CD11bCD18) is also complement receptor 3 (CR3); it binds ICAM-1 and iC3b-opsonized particles.
quote: MAC-1 (αMβ2, CD11bCD18, or complement receptor 3 [CR3]) on circulating monocytes binds to ICAM-1 and mediates adhesion to endothelium

fact: VLA-4 binds VCAM-1 (CD106) on cytokine-activated endothelium.
quote: VLA-4 binds to vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1, CD106), an Ig superfamily protein expressed on cytokine-activated endothelial cells

fact: Chemokine receptor signals change integrin conformation to a high-affinity state; this is called inside-out signalling.
quote: alter the binding functions of the extracellular domain of integrins is called inside-out signaling

fact: Endothelial heparan sulfate proteoglycans bind chemokines and display them to adherent leukocytes.
quote: Chemokines produced in the tissues bind to heparan sulfate proteoglycans on endothelial cells that line postcapillary venules

fact: Leukocyte recruitment follows selectin-mediated rolling, chemokine-mediated integrin activation, stable integrin-mediated arrest and transmigration.
quote: Selectin-mediated rolling of leukocytes on endothelium... Chemokine-mediated increase in affinity of integrins... Stable integrin-mediated arrest... Transmigration of leukocytes through the endothelium

fact: For firm arrest, cytokines upregulate endothelial VCAM-1 (binds VLA-4) and ICAM-1 (binds LFA-1 and MAC-1).
quote: These ligands include VCAM-1, which binds the integrin VLA-4, and ICAM-1, which binds LFA-1 and MAC-1 integrins

fact: Leukocytes usually migrate between endothelial cells; Abbas calls this paracellular transmigration or diapedesis.
quote: Leukocytes usually migrate out of blood vessels between endothelial cells, a process called paracellular transmigration or diapedesis

fact: Transmigration involves CD31 and a reversible disruption of the VE-cadherin junction complex.
quote: notably CD31... This process requires a transient and reversible disruption of adherens junction proteins, primarily the VE-cadherin complex

fact: Janeway uses the term diapedesis for the movement through the basement membrane, after the cell squeezes between endothelial cells using PECAM (CD31).
quote: The movement through the basement membrane is known as diapedesis, and it enables phagocytes to enter the subendothelial tissues.

fact: Chemotaxis is movement of cells along a chemoattractant concentration gradient toward its source.
quote: Chemokines stimulate movement of cells along the concentration gradient of the secreted proteins toward their source, a process called chemotaxis

fact: CXC chemokines with an ELR motif support neutrophil migration.
quote: CXC chemokines with ELR motifs support neutrophil migration.

fact: Chemokine receptors are seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
quote: The receptors for chemokines belong to the seven-transmembrane, guanosine triphosphate-binding (G) protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) superfamily.

fact: Neutrophils express CXCR1 and CXCR2, which bind CXCL1 and CXCL8 (IL-8).
quote: Neutrophils express CXCR1 and CXCR2, which bind CXCL1 and CXCL8 (IL-8), the major chemokines with ELR motifs

fact: Classical monocytes express CCR2; its most important ligand for monocyte recruitment is CCL2 (MCP-1).
quote: classical monocytes... express CCR2. This receptor binds several chemokines, the most important one for monocyte recruitment being CCL2 (MCP-1)

fact: C5a, C3a and leukotriene B4 (LTB4) are chemoattractants for phagocytes and act through GPCRs.
quote: The C3a and C5a complement fragments... and the arachidonic acid metabolite leukotriene B4 (LTB4) are important chemoattractants that promote phagocyte migration

fact: Formyl peptide receptor 1 (FPR1) recognizes N-formylmethionyl bacterial peptides, which are among the most potent leukocyte chemoattractants.
quote: The bacterial peptide ligands that bind this receptor are some of the most potent known chemoattractants for leukocytes.

fact: The fMLP receptor is a GPCR; its signals direct cell movement and induce reactive oxygen species in the phagolysosome.
quote: Signaling through the fMLP receptor also induces the production of microbicidal reactive oxygen species in the phagolysosome.

fact: Neutrophils exposed to C5a or CXCL8 are activated to produce the respiratory burst.
quote: neutrophils exposed to C5a or CXCL8 are activated to produce the respiratory burst that generates oxygen radicals and nitric oxide

fact: Neutrophils are usually the most numerous leukocytes in tissue within 24 to 48 hours of infection and are then replaced by monocytes.
quote: neutrophils are usually the most numerous type of leukocyte to accumulate in tissues, within 24 to 48 hours after the onset of an infection

fact: Janeway states that neutrophil influx usually peaks within the first 6 hours of an inflammatory response.
quote: Their influx usually peaks within the first 6 hours of an inflammatory response, whereas monocytes can be recruited later, through the action of CCL2.

fact: An adult makes more than 1 x 10^11 neutrophils per day; each circulates from a few hours to up to 5 days.
quote: produces more than 1 × 10^11 neutrophils per day, each of which circulates in the blood from a few hours to up to 5 days

fact: Neutrophil life span in tissues is 1 to 2 days; tissue-resident macrophages can live for years.
quote: Life span in tissues 1–2 days ... Tissue-resident macrophages: years

fact: Neutrophil production is stimulated by G-CSF and GM-CSF.
quote: Production of neutrophils is stimulated by granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF).

fact: Neutrophil specific granules contain lysozyme, collagenase and elastase; azurophilic granules contain myeloperoxidase, defensins and cathelicidins.
quote: specific granules, are filled with enzymes, such as lysozyme, collagenase, and elastase... azurophilic granules... contain enzymes (e.g., myeloperoxidase)

fact: Dead and dying neutrophils are a major component of pus.
quote: Dead and dying neutrophils are a major component of the pus that forms in abscesses

fact: Phagocytosis is an active, energy-dependent engulfment of particles larger than 0.5 micrometre.
quote: Phagocytosis is an active, energy-dependent process of engulfment of large particles (greater than 0.5 μm in diameter) into vesicles.

fact: Binding of the microbe to phagocyte receptors is the first step of phagocytosis; some are PRRs such as C-type lectins and scavenger receptors.
quote: binding of microbes to these receptors is the first step in phagocytosis... pattern recognition receptors, including C-type lectins and scavenger receptors

fact: Opsonization is the coating of a pathogen with antibodies and/or complement proteins so that phagocytes take it up more readily.
quote: Opsonization refers to the coating of a pathogen by antibodies and/or complement proteins so that it is more readily taken up

fact: FcγRI (CD64) is a high-affinity IgG receptor on macrophages and neutrophils; it binds IgG1 and IgG3 and mediates phagocytosis.
quote: FcγRI (CD64) High (Kd ~10−9 M); binds IgG1 and IgG3, can bind monomeric IgG ... Phagocytosis; activation of phagocytes

fact: CR1 (CD35) is a high-affinity receptor for C3b and C4b; phagocytes use it to bind and internalize opsonized particles.
quote: CR1 is a high-affinity receptor for C3b and C4b... Phagocytes use this receptor to bind and internalize particles opsonized with C3b or C4b.

fact: CR1 alone is inefficient at inducing phagocytosis; simultaneous IgG-FcγR binding or IFN-γ activation enhances it.
quote: By itself, CR1 is inefficient at inducing the phagocytosis of C3b-coated microbes, but its ability to do so is enhanced

fact: C5a can activate macrophages to ingest bacteria bound to CR1.
quote: the small complement fragment C5a can activate macrophages to ingest bacteria bound to their CR1 receptors

fact: CR3 (MAC-1, CD11bCD18) is an integrin receptor for iC3b; its beta chain CD18 is shared with LFA-1 and CR4.
quote: The type 3 complement receptor, also called MAC-1 (CR3, CD11bCD18), is an integrin that functions as a receptor for the iC3b fragment

fact: CR3 also directly recognizes and phagocytoses microbes that bear beta-glucans.
quote: The complement receptor CR3 also directly recognizes and phagocytoses microbes bearing B-glucans.

fact: The membrane cup closes around the particle to form a phagosome, which fuses with a lysosome.
quote: the top of the cup closes over and pinches off the interior of the cup to form an inside-out intracellular vesicle

fact: Fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes forms phagolysosomes, where most microbicidal mechanisms are concentrated.
quote: The fusion of phagocytic vacuoles (phagosomes) with lysosomes results in the formation of phagolysosomes, where most of the microbicidal mechanisms are concentrated.

fact: Signals from TLRs, Fc and C3b receptors, IFN-γ receptors and CD40 activate phagocytes to kill ingested microbes.
quote: pattern recognition receptors (such as TLRs), opsonin receptors (such as Fc and C3b receptors), receptors for cytokines (mainly IFN-γ), and CD40

fact: The three most important classes of microbicidal molecules are reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide and proteolytic enzymes.
quote: Three classes of microbicidal molecules are known to be the most important.

fact: Phagocyte (NADPH) oxidase is a multisubunit enzyme assembled mainly in the phagolysosomal membrane of activated phagocytes.
quote: Phagocyte oxidase is a multisubunit enzyme that is assembled in activated phagocytes, mainly in the phagolysosomal membrane.

fact: Phagocyte oxidase reduces molecular oxygen to superoxide, with NADPH as cofactor.
quote: to chemically reduce molecular oxygen into ROS, such as superoxide radicals, with the reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) acting as a cofactor

fact: Superoxide is dismutated to hydrogen peroxide; myeloperoxidase uses hydrogen peroxide to convert halide ions into toxic hypohalous acids.
quote: Superoxide is enzymatically dismutated into hydrogen peroxide, which is used by the enzyme myeloperoxidase to convert normally unreactive halide ions into reactive hypohalous acids

fact: The process is called the respiratory burst because it requires oxygen consumption.
quote: The process by which ROS are produced is called the respiratory burst because it requires oxygen consumption

fact: Cytochrome b558 subunits (gp91 and p22) sit in secondary granule membranes; p40, p47 and p67 are cytosolic in resting neutrophils.
quote: subunits (gp91 and gp22) of the NADPH oxidase are localized in the membranes of secondary granules; the other oxidase components (p40, p47, and p67)

fact: fMLP and C5a receptor signals activate Rac2, which is needed for NADPH oxidase assembly.
quote: activating Ras-family GTPases, such as Rac2, that are necessary for the assembly of the active NADPH oxidase

fact: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide; further reactions produce hypochlorite and hydroxyl radical.
quote: O2- is converted by superoxide dismutase (SOD) to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)... to microbicidal hypochlorite (OCl-) and the hydroxyl (•OH) radical

fact: Potassium and hydrogen ions enter the phagolysosome after superoxide forms; this releases and activates granule enzymes such as cathepsin G and elastase.
quote: Potassium and hydrogen ions are then drawn into the phagolysosome... Acidification dissociates granule enzymes such as cathepsin G and elastase

fact: Janeway notes that ROS alone may not kill; ROS-driven K+ influx raises vacuole pH to the optimum for microbicidal proteins.
quote: ROS cause an influx of K+ ions into the phagocytic vacuole, increasing the pH to the optimal level for the action of microbicidal peptides

fact: Inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is absent in resting macrophages and is induced by TLR signals, especially with IFN-γ.
quote: absent in resting macrophages but is induced in response to microbial products that activate TLRs, especially in combination with IFN-γ

fact: iNOS converts arginine to citrulline and releases NO; NO combines with H2O2 or superoxide to form peroxynitrite.
quote: iNOS catalyzes the conversion of arginine to citrulline and freely diffusible NO gas is released... to produce highly reactive peroxynitrite radicals

fact: Neutrophils make low or no nitric oxide; macrophages make it after iNOS induction.
quote: Nitric oxide Low levels or none Induced after transcriptional activation of iNOS

fact: Elastase and cathepsin G are important neutrophil proteolytic enzymes for bacterial killing.
quote: One of the important enzymes in neutrophils is elastase, a broad-spectrum serine protease... Another important enzyme is cathepsin G.

fact: Defensins are cationic peptides made by epithelia and by neutrophils; they kill microbes mainly by disrupting microbial membranes.
quote: Defensins are produced by epithelial cells of mucosal surfaces and by granule-containing leukocytes, including neutrophils

fact: Neutrophil alpha-defensins are stored in primary granules, which fuse with phagosomes.
quote: generating a mature cationic defensin that is stored in the so-called primary granules

fact: Lysozyme digests cell walls of some Gram-positive bacteria; lactoferrin sequesters iron.
quote: Lysozyme: digests cell walls of some Gram-positive bacteria ... Lactoferrin (sequesters Fe2+)

fact: NETs are extruded DNA and histone strands with bound granule proteins (lysozyme, elastase, defensins) that trap and kill bacteria and fungi.
quote: are composed of strands of DNA and histones to which high concentrations of antimicrobial granule contents are bound, including lysozyme, elastase, and defensins

fact: NET formation needs PAD4-mediated histone citrullination, elastase, myeloperoxidase and phagocyte oxidase.
quote: NET formation requires citrullination of histones by the enzyme peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD4), as well as neutrophil serine protease elastase, myeloperoxidase, and phagocyte oxidase

fact: NET extrusion usually causes neutrophil death (NETosis); excessive NET formation contributes to autoimmune and inflammatory disease.
quote: usually leads to neutrophil cell death, referred to as NETosis... excessive NET formation contributes to autoimmune and other inflammatory diseases

fact: Phagocyte defects cause invasive bacterial or fungal infections of skin, liver and respiratory tract, mainly Aspergillus and Candida for fungi.
quote: invasive infections of the skin, liver, and respiratory tract with bacteria or fungi, the latter predominantly involving Aspergillus and Candida species

fact: Janeway groups phagocyte defects into defects of production, adhesion, activation and killing.
quote: deficiencies in phagocyte production, phagocyte adhesion, phagocyte activation, and phagocyte killing of microorganisms

fact: Flow cytometry can detect absence of a cell-surface or intracellular protein in immunodeficiency work-up.
quote: flow cytometric analysis of immune cells to evaluate numbers and relative proportions of these cells or the absence of a cell surface or intracellular protein

fact: CGD is caused by mutations in components of NADPH oxidase (phagocyte oxidase).
quote: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is caused by mutations in components of the NADPH oxidase (also called phagocyte oxidase) enzyme complex.

fact: About two-thirds of CGD cases are X-linked recessive (gp91, the 91-kD subunit of cytochrome b558); the rest are autosomal recessive.
quote: Approximately two-thirds of cases show an X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance, and the remainder are autosomal recessive.

fact: CGD affects about 1 in 200,000 individuals in the United States.
quote: estimated to affect approximately 1 in 200,000 individuals in the United States

fact: Autosomal recessive CGD (other oxidase subunits) can be milder, with later onset.
quote: Autosomal mutations in other subunits of the NADPH oxidase can also cause chronic granulomatous disease, but can be milder and have a later onset.

fact: Invasive Aspergillus infection is the leading cause of death in CGD.
quote: Invasive infection with the fungus Aspergillus is the leading cause of death.

fact: Catalase-producing organisms such as Staphylococcus are troublesome in CGD because catalase destroys the hydrogen peroxide from residual host superoxide.
quote: such as Staphylococcus, produce catalase, which destroys the microbicidal hydrogen peroxide that may be produced by host cells from residual superoxide

fact: In CGD, uncontrolled infection drives T cell-mediated macrophage activation and granuloma formation.
quote: they stimulate chronic cell-mediated immune responses, resulting in T cell-mediated macrophage activation and the formation of granulomas

fact: CGD management includes antibiotic and antifungal prophylaxis, IFN-γ, and consideration of HSCT; gene therapy trials are ongoing.
quote: Treatment with the cytokine IFN-γ can be used in addition to preventive antibiotic and antifungal therapy... standard of care to consider hematopoietic stem cell transplantation

fact: After HSCT, restoring neutrophil superoxide production to at least 15% of normal greatly improves resistance to infection.
quote: If neutrophil superoxide production is restored to at least 15% of normal levels after HSCT, resistance to infection is greatly improved.

fact: Secondary HLH can complicate CGD.
quote: Secondary HLH can also be seen as a complication of CGD

fact: Myeloperoxidase deficiency impairs intracellular killing and gives a CGD-like but less severe phenotype.
quote: Deficiencies in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and myeloperoxidase also impair intracellular bacterial killing and lead to a similar, although less severe, phenotype.

fact: Janeway lists G6PD deficiency and myeloperoxidase deficiency, with CGD, as defects of the respiratory burst.
quote: The respiratory burst is defective in chronic granulomatous disease, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, and myeloperoxidase deficiency.

fact: LADs are autosomal recessive; they cause failure of neutrophil recruitment, severe early bacterial infections and inability to make pus.
quote: The leukocyte adhesion deficiencies are a group of autosomal recessive disorders... severe bacterial infections starting early in life, and an inability to make pus

fact: LAD-1 is caused by CD18 mutations with absent or reduced beta2 integrins (LFA-1, MAC-1, p150,95).
quote: absent or reduced expression of the β2 integrins... as a result of mutations in the CD18 gene

fact: LAD-1 causes recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, impaired wound healing and common leukocytosis.
quote: characterized by recurrent bacterial and fungal infections and impaired wound healing. Leukocytosis is common

fact: In LAD-1, adherence, aggregation, chemotaxis, phagocytosis and cytotoxicity of leukocytes are defective.
quote: including adherence to endothelium, neutrophil aggregation and chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and cytotoxicity mediated by neutrophils, NK cells, and T lymphocytes

fact: LAD-2 is caused by a defective GDP-fucose transporter; sialyl Lewis X is absent and leukocytes do not roll.
quote: caused by a mutation in a guanosine diphosphate (GDP)-fucose transporter... the absence of leukocyte rolling

fact: LAD-2 also causes severe developmental abnormalities and the Bombay blood group phenotype; it is a congenital disorder of glycosylation.
quote: This abnormality in fucosylation seen in LAD-2 also contributes to a Bombay blood group phenotype

fact: LAD-3 is caused mainly by KINDLIN-3 mutations that block inside-out chemokine-induced integrin activation.
quote: This deficiency is caused by a defect in the inside-out signaling pathway that mediates chemokine-induced integrin activation

fact: LAD-3 causes a life-threatening bleeding disorder from defective platelet aggregation, with normal platelet counts.
quote: a life-threatening bleeding disorder that requires blood transfusions because of defective platelet aggregation, even though blood platelet counts are normal

fact: Infections in LAD resist antibiotic treatment and show impaired wound healing and no pus.
quote: impaired wound healing and, in pyogenic bacterial infections, the absence of pus formation. The infections that occur in these patients are resistant to antibiotic treatment

fact: Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (CHS) is autosomal recessive with pyogenic infections, partial oculocutaneous albinism and giant lysosomes in leukocytes.
quote: recurrent infections by pyogenic bacteria, partial oculocutaneous albinism... The neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes of these patients contain giant lysosomes.

fact: CHS is caused by mutations in LYST, which regulates intracellular trafficking of lysosomes.
quote: caused by mutations in the gene encoding the protein LYST, which regulates intracellular trafficking of lysosomes

fact: In CHS, NK cell function is impaired and leukocytes show defective chemotaxis and phagocytosis.
quote: NK cell function in these patients is impaired... Leukocytes are also defective in chemotaxis and phagocytosis

fact: Untransplanted CHS patients usually develop hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) with fever, DIC, organomegaly and hemophagocytosis.
quote: CHS patients who are not transplanted will likely develop a life-threatening syndrome that includes fever, disseminated intravascular coagulation

fact: In CHS, phagosomes and lysosomes fail to fuse properly; phagocytes have enlarged granules and poor intracellular killing.
quote: causes a failure of lysosomes and phagosomes to fuse properly; the phagocytes in these patients have enlarged granules and impaired intracellular killing ability

fact: CHS features metallic silver hair, poor vision and platelet dysfunction with bleeding.
quote: The hair is typically a metallic silver color, vision is poor because of abnormalities in retinal pigment cells, and platelet dysfunction causes increased bleeding.

fact: Severe congenital neutropenia (SCN, Kostmann disease) has a persistent neutrophil count below 0.5 x 10^9/L.
quote: the neutrophil count is persistently less than 0.5 x 10^9 per liter of blood

fact: Cyclic neutropenia has neutrophil counts that fluctuate with a cycle of about 21 days.
quote: neutrophil numbers that fluctuate from near normal to very low or undetectable, with an approximate cycle time of 21 days

fact: Mutations in ELA2 (neutrophil elastase) are the most common cause of SCN; some ELA2 mutations cause cyclic neutropenia.
quote: sporadic or autosomal dominant mutations of the gene that encodes neutrophil elastase (ELA2)... Some mutations of ELA2 cause cyclic neutropenia

fact: HAX1 deficiency causes an autosomal recessive form of SCN.
quote: Autosomal recessive forms of SCN have also been identified. Deficiency of the mitochondrial protein HAX1 leads to increased apoptosis

fact: SCN and cyclic neutropenia carry an increased risk of myelodysplasia or myeloid leukemia; G-CSF is the mainstay of treatment.
quote: increased risk of developing myelodysplasia or myeloid leukemia... G-CSF which is now the mainstay of treatment for congenital neutropenias

fact: MSMD is severe disease from weakly virulent mycobacteria and other intracellular pathogens such as Salmonella; BCG vaccine can disseminate.
quote: predisposed to severe disease caused by weakly virulent mycobacteria that do not cause disease in healthy individuals... the vaccine can cause disseminated mycobacterial infection

fact: MSMD genes include IL-12p40, IL-12Rbeta1, both IFN-γ receptor chains, STAT1 and NEMO (IKKγ).
quote: Mutations in the genes encoding IL-12p40, the IL-12Rβ1 chain, and both chains of the IFN-γ receptor, as well as some mutations in STAT1 and IKKγ

fact: IL-12 from DCs and macrophages drives IFN-γ production by T cells and NK cells.
quote: IL-12R signaling stimulates the synthesis of IFN-γ by helper T cells, cytotoxic T cells, and NK cells

fact: Because p40 is shared by IL-12 and IL-23, p40 deficiency causes both IL-12 and IL-23 deficiency.
quote: p40 is shared by IL-12 and IL-23, and so p40 deficiency can cause both IL-12 and IL-23 deficiency.

fact: Total absence of IFN-γ receptor expression markedly reduces granuloma formation.
quote: In the total absence of IFN-y receptor expression, granuloma formation is much reduced

fact: MyD88 or IRAK4 deficiency causes severe pyogenic infections with little inflammation ('cold' infections).
quote: recurrent, severe peripheral, and invasive infections by pyogenic bacteria that elicit little inflammation, a situation known as a 'cold' infection

fact: Genetic testing is often used relatively early in the diagnosis of inborn errors of immunity.
quote: genetics is often used relatively early in diagnosis, compared to other clinical disciplines

fact: Janeway places neutrophil elastase (ELA2) in the azurophilic granules.
quote: encodes neutrophil elastase (ELA2), a component of the azurophilic granules

fact: Janeway states that neutrophil cathelicidin propeptides are stored in secondary granules and are activated by elastase released from primary granules.
quote: the cathelicidin propeptides are stored in the secondary granules... encounter neutrophil elastase that has been released from primary granules

fact: Janeway describes four steps of extravasation: selectin rolling, tight integrin binding, crossing the endothelium and basement membrane, and migration through tissue along chemokine gradients.
quote: The migration of leukocytes out of blood vessels, the process known as extravasation, is thought to occur in four steps.

fact: In CGD, loss of NADPH oxidase activity causes defective superoxide production, so phagocytes fail to kill ingested microbes.
quote: The loss of NADPH oxidase activity results in defective production of superoxide anion... results in a failure to kill phagocytosed microbes.

fact: Complement is a major effector mechanism of humoral immunity and also an important effector mechanism of innate immunity.
quote: one of the major effector mechanisms of humoral immunity and is also an important effector mechanism of innate immunity

fact: Complement proteases circulate as inactive zymogens and become active only after proteolytic cleavage.
quote: synthesized as inactive pro-enzymes, or zymogens, which only become enzymatically active after proteolytic cleavage

fact: Each activated complement protease cleaves many molecules of the next zymogen, so the signal amplifies at each step.
quote: each becoming an active protease that cleaves and activates many molecules of the next zymogen in the pathway

fact: The larger cleavage fragment gets the suffix b and the smaller fragment gets the suffix a; C2 is the one exception.
quote: The larger fragment is always designated by the suffix b, with one exception.

fact: For C2, the larger fragment that stays attached is called C2a and the released smaller fragment is called C2b.
quote: because the attached, larger fragment is called the a piece and the released part is the b fragment

fact: The proteins are numbered in order of discovery, not order of action; the classical pathway reaction sequence is C1, C4, C2, C3, C5, C6, C7, C8 and C9.
quote: named in the order of their discovery rather than the sequence of reactions. The reaction sequence in the classical pathway

fact: Three pathways activate complement: the classical pathway (antibody bound to antigen), the alternative pathway (microbial surfaces without antibody) and the lectin pathway (lectins that bind microbial carbohydrates).
quote: the classical pathway, which is activated by certain classes of antibodies bound to antigens; the alternative pathway

fact: The alternative and lectin pathways are innate effector mechanisms; the classical pathway is a major mechanism of adaptive humoral immunity.
quote: The alternative and lectin pathways are effector mechanisms of innate immunity, whereas the classical pathway is a major mechanism of adaptive humoral immunity.

fact: All three pathways can start without antibody, as part of innate immunity.
quote: All three pathways can be initiated independently of antibody as part of innate immunity.

fact: The central event of complement activation is cleavage of C3 by a C3 convertase into C3a and C3b, with covalent attachment of C3b to the target surface.
quote: The central event in complement activation is proteolysis of the complement protein C3

fact: Cleavage of C3 exposes a reactive thioester bond in C3b; if C3b does not bond to a nearby surface, the thioester is hydrolyzed and C3b becomes inactive.
quote: If no bond is made, the thioester is rapidly hydrolyzed, inactivating C3b.

fact: Regulatory proteins on normal host cells inhibit complement activation; microbes lack these proteins, so activation proceeds on microbial surfaces.
quote: Complement activation is inhibited by regulatory proteins that are present on normal host cells and absent from microbes.

fact: The classical pathway starts when C1 binds the CH2 domain of IgG or the CH3 domain of IgM that has bound antigen.
quote: binding of the complement protein C1 to the CH2 domains of IgG or the CH3 domains of IgM

fact: Among human IgG subclasses, IgG1 and IgG3 are the most efficient complement activators.
quote: Among IgG antibodies, IgG1 and IgG3 (in humans) are more efficient activators of complement than are other subclasses.

fact: IgG2 activates complement weakly and IgG4 does not activate complement.
quote: IgG2 has some ability to activate complement, but IgG4 does not.

fact: C1 consists of C1q, which binds antibody, and C1r and C1s, which are serine proteases.
quote: C1q binds to the antibody, and C1r and C1s are proteases

fact: Each C1q must bind at least two Ig heavy chains to be activated, so only antigen-bound antibody, not free antibody, activates the classical pathway.
quote: each C1q molecule must bind to at least two Ig heavy chains to be activated

fact: One antigen-bound IgM molecule can bind two or more C1q molecules, so IgM fixes complement more efficiently than IgG.
quote: a single molecule of IgM can bind two or more C1q molecules

fact: C1q also binds pentraxins such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and serum amyloid P, and it binds apoptotic bodies.
quote: C1q also binds to pentraxins like C-reactive protein and serum amyloid protein, and can also bind to apoptotic bodies

fact: Binding of C1q activates C1r; C1r cleaves and activates C1s; C1s cleaves C4, and C4b binds covalently to the surface through its thioester bond.
quote: enzymatic activation of the associated C1r, which cleaves and activates C1s

fact: C2 binds surface C4b and is cleaved by C1s; the larger C2a fragment stays bound to C4b.
quote: a larger C2a fragment that remains physically associated with C4b on the cell surface

fact: C4b2a is the classical pathway C3 convertase.
quote: The resulting C4b2a complex is the classical pathway C3 convertase

fact: C3b binds to C4b2a to form C4b2a3b, the classical pathway C5 convertase.
quote: form a C4b2a3b complex. This complex functions as the classical pathway C5 convertase

fact: C3 is homologous to C4, and factor B is homologous to C2.
quote: C3 in the alternative pathway is homologous to C4 in the classical pathway, and Factor B is homologous to C2.

fact: The lectin pathway starts when plasma mannose-binding lectin (MBL) or ficolins bind microbial polysaccharides.
quote: triggered by the binding of microbial polysaccharides to circulating lectins, such as plasma mannose-binding lectin (MBL), or to ficolins

fact: MBL binds mannose residues on microbial polysaccharides.
quote: MBL binds to mannose residues on polysaccharides

fact: Ficolins (L-, H- and M-ficolin) bind N-acetylglucosamine-containing glycans through a fibrinogen-like domain.
quote: the fibrinogen-like domain of ficolin binds N-acetylglucosamine–containing glycans

fact: MASP1 may activate MASP2, and MASP2 cleaves C4 and C2.
quote: MASP1 may activate MASP2 and MASP2 is the protease that cleaves C4 and C2

fact: The lectin pathway forms the same C3 convertase as the classical pathway, C4b2a.
quote: forming C4b2a, which is the C3 convertase of the lectin pathway

fact: Plasma C3 is cleaved spontaneously at a low rate of 1-2% of total C3 per hour (C3 tick-over).
quote: continuously cleaved at a low rate (1%–2% of the total plasma C3 per hour)

fact: Tick-over gives C3(H2O), which binds factor B; factor D then cleaves factor B and a short-lived fluid-phase C3 convertase, C3(H2O)Bb, forms.
quote: producing a short-lived fluid-phase C3 convertase, C3(H,O)Bb

fact: Surface C3b binds factor B, factor D cleaves factor B (Ba is released, Bb stays), and C3bBb forms the alternative pathway C3 convertase.
quote: The C3bBb complex is the alternative pathway C3 convertase

fact: The alternative pathway C3 convertase amplifies complement activation that starts by the alternative, classical or lectin pathway.
quote: the alternative pathway C3 convertase functions to amplify complement activation when it is initiated by the alternative, classical, or lectin pathway

fact: Factor D is the only activating protease of complement that circulates as an active enzyme, not as a zymogen.
quote: the only activating protease of the complement system to circulate as an active enzyme rather than a zymogen

fact: Properdin binds and stabilizes C3bBb, and it attaches preferentially to microbial surfaces.
quote: properdin, can bind to and stabilize the C3bBb complex, and the attachment of properdin is favored on microbial as opposed to normal host cells

fact: The alternative pathway C5 convertase contains one Bb and two C3b molecules (C3bBb3b).
quote: a complex containing one Bb moiety and two molecules of C3b, which functions as the alternative pathway C5 convertase

fact: Janeway writes the C5 convertases as C4b2a3b (classical and lectin) and C3b2Bb (alternative).
quote: C3b binds both to C4b2a and C3bBb, forming the active C5 convertases C4b2a3b and C3b,Bb

fact: C5 binds to the C3b part of a C5 convertase and is cleaved by C2a or Bb.
quote: rendered susceptible to cleavage by the serine protease activity of C2a or Bb

fact: Unlike C3b and C4b, C5b does not bind covalently to the cell surface.
quote: Unlike C3b and C4b, C5b is not covalently bound to the cell surface.

fact: C5b binds C6 and then C7; the C5b-7 complex inserts into the lipid bilayer.
quote: C7 from the plasma then binds to the α chain of C5b and forms the C5b-C6-C7 (C5b-7) complex

fact: C8 binds to form C5b-8, which makes small, unstable pores of 0.4-3 nm.
quote: forms unstable pores that range from 0.4 to 3 nm in diameter

fact: Recruitment of the first C9 molecule is the rate-limiting step of MAC formation.
quote: The rate-limiting step in MAC formation is the recruitment of the first C9 molecule

fact: Abbas states that the MAC pore contains C5b, C6, C7, C8 and up to 18 C9 molecules.
quote: C5b-9 complexes containing C5b, C6, C7, C8, and up to 18 molecules of C9

fact: Janeway states that 10-16 C9 molecules polymerize to form the MAC.
quote: the polymerization of 10-16 molecules of C9

fact: Water enters through the MAC pore, and the cell swells and ruptures (osmotic lysis).
quote: The entry of water results in osmotic swelling and rupture of the cells

fact: MAC-mediated lysis is critical for defense against only a few pathogens, such as thin-walled Neisseria.
quote: such as bacteria of the genus Neisseria, which have thin cell walls

fact: Deficiency of C5-C9 is associated with susceptibility only to Neisseria species.
quote: deficiencies in complement components C5-C9 have been associated with susceptibility only to Neisseria species

fact: C3b and C4b bind CR1; iC3b binds CR3 (MAC-1) and CR4.
quote: C3b and C4b (the latter generated by the classical pathway only) bind to CR1, and iC3b binds to CR3 (MAC-1) and CR4

fact: CR1 alone triggers phagocytosis of C3b-coated microbes inefficiently; simultaneous IgG binding to Fc gamma receptors enhances it.
quote: By itself, CR1 is inefficient at inducing the phagocytosis of C3b-coated microbes

fact: Binding of iC3b to CR3 is sufficient on its own to stimulate phagocytosis.
quote: the binding of iC3b to the receptor CR3 is sufficient on its own to stimulate phagocytosis

fact: People without a spleen are susceptible to disseminated pneumococcal and meningococcal septicemia.
quote: are susceptible to disseminated pneumococcal and meningococcal septicemia

fact: C5a, C4a and C3a bind to mast cells and cause degranulation with release of vasoactive mediators such as histamine.
quote: All three peptides bind to mast cells and induce degranulation, with the release of vasoactive mediators, such as histamine.

fact: C3a, C4a and C5a are called anaphylatoxins because the mast cell reactions they trigger are characteristic of anaphylaxis.
quote: These peptides are also called anaphylatoxins because the mast cell reactions they trigger are characteristic of anaphylaxis

fact: C5a is the most potent mediator of mast cell degranulation; C3a is about 20-fold and C4a about 2500-fold less potent.
quote: C5a is the most potent mediator of mast cell degranulation, C3a is approximately 20-fold less potent, and C4a is approximately 2500-fold less

fact: In neutrophils, C5a stimulates motility, firm adhesion to endothelium and, at high doses, the respiratory burst.
quote: C5a stimulates motility, firm adhesion to endothelial cells, and, at high doses, stimulation of the respiratory burst

fact: Large systemic amounts of anaphylatoxins cause circulatory collapse, a shock-like syndrome similar to a systemic IgE-mediated allergic reaction.
quote: they induce a generalized circulatory collapse, producing a shock-like syndrome similar to that seen in a systemic allergic reaction

fact: C3a and C5a can degranulate mast cells without allergen cross-linking of the high-affinity IgE receptor.
quote: The complement fragments C3a and C5a can cause mast cell degranulation, and this is why they were named anaphylatoxins.

fact: C5a is a chemoattractant for eosinophils.
quote: the complement product C5a and the lipid mediators PAF and LTB4 produced by mast cells also function as chemoattractants for eosinophils

fact: The C5a receptor C5aR1 is a G protein-coupled receptor on neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes, macrophages, mast cells and other cells.
quote: C5aR1, is the most thoroughly characterized. It is a member of the G protein–coupled receptor family

fact: Plasma carboxypeptidases remove the C-terminal arginine of C3a and C5a; the des-Arg forms keep only about 10% of the activity.
quote: C3a des-Arg and C5a des-Arg, which each have only approximately 10% of the activity of the native forms

fact: CR1 on erythrocytes binds circulating immune complexes that carry C3b and C4b and carries them to the liver and spleen for removal by phagocytes.
quote: CR1 on erythrocytes binds circulating immune complexes with attached C3b and C4b

fact: CR2 (CD21) binds C3d, C3dg and iC3b; on B cells it forms a complex with CD19 and CD81.
quote: a trimolecular complex that includes two other noncovalently attached proteins called CD19 and CD81

fact: CR2 is the receptor for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).
quote: Receptor for EBV

fact: C3d on an antigen binds CR2 on B cells and facilitates B-cell activation.
quote: The C3d protein generated from C3 binds to CR2 on B cells and facilitates B-cell activation

fact: CR3 (MAC-1, CD11b/CD18) is an integrin that binds iC3b and also ICAM-1 on endothelium.
quote: The type 3 complement receptor, also called MAC-1 (CR3, CD11bCD18), is an integrin

fact: CR4 (CD11c/CD18) also binds iC3b; CD11c is a marker of dendritic cells.
quote: CD11c is abundantly expressed on dendritic cells and is used as a marker for this cell type.

fact: Mutations in the shared CD18 chain remove CR3 and CR4 and cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD).
quote: The disease caused by this gene defect is called leukocyte adhesion deficiency

fact: C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) is a serpin; active C1r2s2 cleaves it, it binds covalently, and C1r2s2 dissociates from C1q.
quote: C1 INH is a serine protease inhibitor (serpin) that mimics the normal substrates of C1r and C1s

fact: C1-INH also inactivates MASP2 and so dampens the lectin pathway.
quote: by inactivating MASP2, C1-INH also dampens the lectin pathway

fact: C1-INH also inhibits kallikrein and coagulation factor XII, which promote bradykinin formation.
quote: C1-INH is an inhibitor of other plasma serine proteases besides C1, including kallikrein and coagulation factor XII

fact: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is an autosomal dominant disease caused by deficiency of C1-INH.
quote: An autosomal dominant inherited disease called hereditary angioedema is due to a deficiency of C1-INH.

fact: The edema mediators in HAE include C2 kinin (a C2 fragment) and bradykinin.
quote: The mediators of edema formation in patients with hereditary angioedema include a proteolytic fragment of C2, called C2 kinin, and bradykinin.

fact: Factor H binds C3b, displaces Bb and is a cofactor for factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b.
quote: Binds C3b and displaces Bb

fact: Factor H blocks only Bb binding to C3b, so it regulates the alternative pathway but not the classical pathway.
quote: Factor H inhibits binding of only Bb to C3b and is thus a regulator of the alternative but not the classical pathway.

fact: Sialic acid-rich host cell surfaces favor binding of factor H over factor B.
quote: cell surfaces rich in sialic acid favor binding of the regulatory protein Factor H over the alternative pathway protein Factor B

fact: C4-binding protein (C4BP) is a plasma protein that binds C4b, displaces C2 and is a cofactor for factor I-mediated cleavage of C4b.
quote: Binds C4b and displaces C2

fact: Factor I is a plasma serine protease that cleaves C3b and C4b, with factor H, MCP, C4BP or CR1 as cofactor.
quote: cleaves C3b and C4b by using factor H, MCP, C4BP, or CR1 as cofactors

fact: Factor I circulates in active form but cleaves C3b and C4b only when they are bound to a cofactor protein.
quote: it circulates in active form but can cleave C3b and C4b only when they are bound to a membrane cofactor protein

fact: Factor I cleavage of C3b generates iC3b, C3d and C3dg; these do not take part in activation but bind receptors on phagocytes and B cells.
quote: Factor I–mediated cleavage of C3b generates the fragments called iC3b, C3d, and C3dg

fact: Membrane cofactor protein (MCP, CD46) is on leukocytes, epithelial cells and endothelial cells and is a cofactor for factor I cleavage of C3b and C4b.
quote: Cofactor for factor I–mediated cleavage of C3b and C4b

fact: Decay-accelerating factor (DAF, CD55) displaces C2a from C4b and Bb from C3b, so it dissociates both C3 convertases.
quote: Displaces C2a from C4b and Bb from C3b (dissociation of C3 convertases)

fact: CR1, DAF and factor H displace Bb from C3b; CR1, MCP and factor H are cofactors for factor I cleavage of C3b.
quote: CR1, DAF, and factor H displace Bb from C3b, and CR1, MCP, and factor H catalyze the cleavage of bound C3b

fact: CD59 is a GPI-linked membrane protein that incorporates into the assembling MAC after C5b-8 insertion and blocks addition of C9.
quote: It works by incorporating itself into assembling MACs after the membrane insertion of C5b-8, thereby inhibiting the subsequent addition of C9 molecules

fact: CD59 is also called protectin.
quote: CD59 or protectin, which inhibits the binding of C9 to the C5b678 complex

fact: Plasma S protein binds soluble C5b-7 complexes and prevents their insertion into bystander cell membranes.
quote: plasma proteins such as S protein, which functions by binding to soluble C5b,6,7 complexes

fact: S protein is also called vitronectin.
quote: vitronectin, also known as S-protein, bind to the C5b67 complex

fact: Failure to make GPI anchors removes DAF and CD59 from blood cells and causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).
quote: results in the failure to express many GPI-linked membrane proteins, including DAF and CD59

fact: Factor I deficiency depletes plasma C3 through unregulated fluid-phase C3 convertase formation and causes pyogenic infections.
quote: In patients with Factor I deficiency, plasma C3 is depleted

fact: In complement-mediated hemolytic-uremic syndrome, the most common mutations are in the factor H gene; MCP mutations also occur.
quote: the most common mutations in this condition are in the Factor H gene

fact: Some microbes, such as Gram-positive bacteria and some fungi, have thick cell walls that prevent binding of complement proteins such as the MAC.
quote: Some microbes express thick cell walls that prevent the binding of complement proteins, such as the MAC.

fact: Many pathogens evade complement by recruiting host regulators, for example factor H through surface sialic acid.
quote: Microbes can evade the complement system by recruiting host complement regulatory proteins.

fact: Janeway states that iC3b is a ligand for CR2, CR3 and CR4, but not for CR1.
quote: producing iC3b, which is a ligand for the complement receptors CR2, CR3 and CR4, but not CR1
